synopsis: The booklet identifies credibility—not tool choice—as the decisive toolchain risk; cited on-road frameworks require documented credibility assessments, but these are not presented as off-road acceptance rules [f200, f6928, f7673, f10411]. The market is modular, combining strong on-road sensor/scenario tooling with heavy-machine terrain/hydraulics tools, yet no single tool has public evidence covering heavy-machine automatic braking across many job-site types and all-weather sensing, and public pricing is largely absent [f195, f8281, f197]. Expert judgment rejects a newcomer achieving coverage of more than 100 site types, all weather and every sensor type by mid-2027, but considers a narrow first-release toolchain feasible if work starts in October 2026 and reuses existing simulators [f1590, f1591]. Most infrastructure can be built before hardware arrives if interfaces are established early, but the architecture must accommodate sensor physics and final correlation requires the real sensor and machine; assumed hardware remains a risk until mid-2027 [f5568, f11916, f12227, f10492]. The four-month validation window cannot be compressed, so scenario catalogs, fleet-data pipelines, tools and credibility evidence should be prepared beforehand [f11923]. Planning should assign explicit ownership of qualification and model credibility, use credibility maturity measures rather than toolchain TRLs, and provide verification and configuration-management evidence; component-level physical testing remains a point of debate in the cited on-road material [f5792, f9536, f8034, f7690].
